analysis.one_liner: Blocks the SEC from requiring companies to disclose any information unless it passes a strict materiality test.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2022 with 8 Republican senators backing it, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in December, and never reached a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Securities and Exchange Commission from adding any new disclosure requirement for publicly traded companies unless the SEC formally finds a reasonable investor would think the information matters to an investment decision. This is aimed at the SEC's pending proposals — most prominently the climate risk disclosure rule — that would make companies report things like greenhouse gas emissions. Notably, the restriction is one-way: the SEC could still remove disclosure requirements without any such finding, so it only makes it harder to add new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, and especially the largest issuers facing the SEC's proposed new rules on climate risk and other non-traditional disclosures. They would avoid compliance costs and keep information like emissions data out of required filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public companies facing new SEC disclosure rules

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the SEC from imposing any new disclosure requirement unless it expressly determines a reasonable investor would consider the information important to an investment decision [S3].
Because the restriction applies only to adding requirements and expressly does not apply to removing existing ones, it makes new disclosure rules harder without making any easier to eliminate [S3].
The scope covers rulemaking under both the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the two statutes under which the SEC writes corporate disclosure rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors — including retirement savers whose money is in public markets — who would get less required information about companies, particularly on climate risk and other matters the SEC judged relevant to disclosure even if not to a single investment decision.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors and retirement savers in public markets

drawbacks.text: The one-way structure means removals are exempt: the SEC could strip disclosure requirements without any materiality finding, but could never add one easily, so the bill functions as a ratchet in companies' favor [S3].

The materiality standard in the bill asks whether a reasonable investor would consider the information important to an investment decision. That test could bar disclosure rules — like the SEC's proposed climate rule — that many investors, including large asset managers voting shareholder proxies, actively want [S3].

Supporters argue the bill prevents the SEC from using its disclosure authority to pursue social or environmental policy rather than investor protection, and that some proposed disclosures impose real compliance costs without clear investment value — the strongest good-faith case for the bill [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs mainly to issuers: lower compliance costs and less required reporting. The cost falls on investors, who would have less required information, and the removal exemption makes the restriction one-sided. It is a genuine limits-on-regulators proposal with a defensible rationale, but the asymmetry — easy to deregulate, hard to regulate — tilts it clearly toward the companies it would cover.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where only a subcommittee held a hearing; it was never scheduled for a full committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Rounds introduced the bill with seven Republican cosponsors on September 29, 2022 [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
On December 13, 2022, the Banking Committee's Subcommittee on Securities, Insurance, and Investment held a hearing on the bill [S5].
No further action followed: the full committee never voted to report the bill, and it never received a floor vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].
The Congress.gov record shows no roll-call vote, no committee report, and no House companion action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies that would have faced the SEC's pending new disclosure mandates — including the proposed climate risk rule — are better off, because the bill's death left the SEC's authority to write disclosure rules intact. Investors who wanted more required information in company filings also came out ahead. Because the bill never advanced, no investor lost anything; the status quo, with the SEC free to require disclosure, was preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies facing proposed new SEC disclosure rules

sides.party_line_note: All eight backers — the sponsor and seven cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never came to a vote that would have shown the chamber's split [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would have blocked the SEC from adding new disclosure requirements — including the pending climate risk disclosure rule — unless they passed a strict materiality test, sparing issuers compliance costs and required reporting. The information companies avoid disclosing is information investors and the public lose. Its one-way design (removals exempt) entrenches that advantage without any offsetting gain for investors.

industries.industry: Asset managers and ESG-focused investment funds
industries.note: Large asset managers and funds that market climate- and sustainability-aware products rely on standardized corporate climate data, which the bill would have made far harder for the SEC to require. Their interest in more disclosure runs alongside investors' interest in more information.

The bill would have stripped the SEC of much of its rulemaking discretion over disclosure, tying it to a materiality test in statute. That power is the tool Congress gave it to protect investors; limiting it limits the agency's ability to act for the public.
